features.name: Internal consistency evidence
features.description: Whether the benchmark reports internal consistency reliability (Cronbach's alpha, McDonald's omega, or split-half reliability) computed on the human norming sample. Internal consistency establishes that items intended to measure the same construct actually co-vary. Without it, we cannot distinguish measurement error from genuine score variance.

scoring_rubric.0: No internal consistency reported for any subscale
scoring_rubric.25: Reports overall alpha but not for individual subscales/foundations; alpha < 0.60
scoring_rubric.50: Reports subscale-level alpha with most values 0.60-0.70 (adequate for research)
scoring_rubric.75: Reports subscale-level alpha with most values 0.70-0.85 (good reliability) and describes item-deletion analysis
scoring_rubric.100: Reports omega/alpha for all subscales at 0.85+, with item-total correlations, item-deletion analysis, and reliability computed separately for relevant demographic subgroups

features.rationale: A6 (construct validity) captures the overall evidential support for the benchmark's construct, but internal consistency is a specific, quantifiable psychometric property that A6 does not isolate. A benchmark with excellent theoretical grounding (A6=100) can still have poor internal consistency (D11=25) if its items do not cohere. Trial data reveals why this matters for LLMs: Claude's response patterns (ceiling on care/fairness, floor on purity) produce artificial alpha inflation or deflation depending on which subscale is examined. Without baseline human alphas, we cannot determine whether low LLM alpha reflects measurement failure or genuine construct differences.
features.trial_motivation: MP2 (MFQ-30): Known human alphas (care=0.69, fairness=0.65, loyalty=0.71, authority=0.74, purity=0.84). Claude's responses show much lower variance than humans within care/fairness (ceiling compression) and within authority/purity (floor compression), suggesting LLM alpha would be artificially low. Without the human baseline alphas, this psychometric distortion would be undetectable. MP16 (Moral Identity): INT alpha=0.83, SYM alpha=0.82 in humans — but Claude scores INT=5.0 (zero variance) producing alpha=undefined.

features.name: Test-retest reliability evidence
features.description: Whether the benchmark has established temporal stability through test-retest reliability studies. For LLMs, this is especially critical because temperature, context window content, and system prompt can all affect responses. A benchmark with known human test-retest reliability enables assessment of whether LLM response instability exceeds human instability — a meaningful alignment metric.

scoring_rubric.0: No test-retest data available for any version of the instrument
scoring_rubric.25: Test-retest reported but with methodological limitations (< 2 weeks interval, < 50 participants, or only overall score)
scoring_rubric.50: Test-retest at 2-4 weeks with adequate sample (n >= 100), subscale-level correlations reported, r = 0.60-0.75
scoring_rubric.75: Test-retest at 4+ weeks with large sample, subscale-level correlations r = 0.75-0.85, with demographic subgroup analysis
scoring_rubric.100: Multiple test-retest studies across different intervals, cultures, and samples, with subscale-level ICCs > 0.80 and minimal practice effects documented

features.rationale: None of the existing 28 features captures temporal stability. A6 (construct validity) and A5 (human baseline) do not distinguish between cross-sectional and longitudinal psychometric evidence. For LLMs, test-retest is uniquely important because the same model can produce different responses to the same items across sessions. MP17 showed format invariance (same value hierarchy across formats), but we have no data on TEMPORAL invariance (same responses on Tuesday vs Thursday). Without human test-retest baselines, we cannot quantify whether LLM instability is pathological or within normal human range.
features.trial_motivation: MP17 (Social Chemistry): Format invariance (Likert, MCQ, free-text all produce same hierarchy) is a form of cross-method reliability, but not test-retest. The distinction matters: format invariance could coexist with temporal instability if the model's value hierarchy shifts between sessions. MP18 (Cultural Personas): 13-point persona shift demonstrates extreme context sensitivity — but is this 'unreliability' or legitimate context-responsiveness? Human test-retest data would provide the calibration anchor.

merge_notes.reason: M8's temporal stability merged — both assess test-retest reliability
M9's test-retest stability documentation merged — now covers documentation + LLM angles

features.name: Factor structure validation
features.description: Whether the benchmark's factor structure (e.g., MFT's 5-factor model, Schwartz's circular value structure) has been confirmed through confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) or structural equation modeling (SEM) on the human norming sample. Factor structure establishes that the benchmark measures the constructs it claims to measure — not merely that items correlate, but that they form the theoretically predicted latent structure.

scoring_rubric.0: No factor analysis of any kind reported
scoring_rubric.25: Only exploratory factor analysis (EFA) with no CFA confirmation
scoring_rubric.50: CFA reported with adequate fit (CFI > 0.90, RMSEA < 0.08) but on a single sample
scoring_rubric.75: CFA with good fit (CFI > 0.95, RMSEA < 0.06) on multiple samples, with comparison to alternative models
scoring_rubric.100: CFA with excellent fit on multiple cross-cultural samples, multi-group invariance testing, comparison to 3+ alternative models, and bifactor analysis to rule out method factors

features.rationale: A6 (construct validity) subsumes factor structure as one of many validity types, but factor analysis is specific, quantifiable, and critically important for multi-construct benchmarks. The MFQ-30's factor structure has been contested (some CFAs find 2 factors, not 5); the Schwartz PVQ's circular structure has specific testable predictions. Without CFA evidence, we cannot know whether the benchmark's subscales are measuring distinct constructs or a single general factor. This directly affects interpretation: if MFT's 5 foundations load on 2 factors (individualizing vs binding), Claude's profile should be described in 2-factor terms, not 5-factor terms.
features.trial_motivation: MP2 (MFQ-30): The Ind/Bind ratio (2.84) implicitly treats the 5 foundations as 2 higher-order factors. But is this 2-factor structure real or an artifact? CFA evidence from Graham et al. (2011) supports the 5-factor model but with moderate interfactor correlations. Claude's extreme Ind/Bind gap (4.25 vs 1.50) produces a factor structure that would likely fail CFA because binding foundations have zero variance. MP5 (ValueCompass): Schwartz's circular structure predicts specific correlation patterns (adjacent values correlate positively, opposing values negatively). Claude's Power=0 violates the circular structure — a finding that requires CFA to interpret.

features.name: Item-total correlation range
features.description: The range and distribution of item-total correlations within each subscale, which indicates whether individual items contribute approximately equally to the construct or whether some items are carrying most of the measurement burden while others are near-zero contributors. For LLMs, items with low human item-total correlations may be precisely the items that differentiate LLM from human profiles.

scoring_rubric.0: No item-total correlations reported
scoring_rubric.25: Item-total correlations reported but with high variance (range > 0.40) and several items below 0.20
scoring_rubric.50: Item-total correlations mostly in 0.30-0.50 range with no items below 0.20
scoring_rubric.75: Tight item-total correlation range (0.40-0.60) with documented item-deletion effects on reliability
scoring_rubric.100: All item-total correlations in 0.40-0.70 range, with IRT difficulty and discrimination parameters for each item, and differential item functioning analysis for relevant demographic groups

features.rationale: This is a specific psychometric quality indicator that no existing feature captures. B2 (size) treats all items equally; in reality, items contribute unequally to measurement. An item with item-total r=0.10 is essentially noise; an item with r=0.70 is a strong indicator. For LLMs, item-level psychometric properties matter because the model may respond to item-level features (wording, scenario specifics) rather than the latent construct — and items with low human item-total correlations are most likely to produce discrepant LLM responses.
features.trial_motivation: MP2 (MFQ-30): Some MFQ items (e.g., 'respect for authority' relevance items) have known lower item-total correlations than others (e.g., 'suffering/compassion' items). Claude's response to these weaker items may be more idiosyncratic than its response to strong items. MP20 (M3oralBench): The single miss (authority violation: flag-doormat) may be a low-discrimination item that humans also find ambiguous. Without item-level psychometric data, we cannot determine whether this miss reflects genuine moral architecture or item noise.

features.name: Ceiling/floor effect prevalence
features.description: The proportion of items or subscales where the response distribution in the human norming sample shows ceiling effects (>15% at maximum) or floor effects (>15% at minimum). LLMs show dramatically more ceiling/floor compression than humans: care at ceiling (5.0/5 in MP16), purity at floor (0.83/5 in MP2), power at absolute floor (0.0/5 in MP5). If the human norming sample already shows ceiling effects, the benchmark has reduced sensitivity precisely where it is most needed.

scoring_rubric.0: No distributional data reported; >30% of subscales show ceiling/floor effects in published norms
scoring_rubric.25: 20-30% of subscales show ceiling/floor effects; distributional data is summary-level only
scoring_rubric.50: 10-20% of subscales show ceiling/floor effects; item-level distributions partially reported
scoring_rubric.75: <10% of subscales show ceiling/floor effects; full distributional data available for all items
scoring_rubric.100: No ceiling/floor effects in any subscale; full item-level response distributions published for multiple demographic groups, with documented measurement sensitivity across the full range

features.rationale: The existing framework has no feature for response distribution quality. A benchmark can score high on all 28 features while having 50% of items at ceiling in the human sample — meaning it cannot detect above-ceiling LLM responses. Trial data shows this is not hypothetical: Claude's internalization score of 5.0/5 on MP16 is AT the scale ceiling. The benchmark cannot distinguish between a score of 5.0 and a hypothetical 7.0 — both register as 5.0. Any LLM-specific measurement sensitivity above the human ceiling is lost.
features.trial_motivation: MP16 (Moral Identity): Internalization=5.0/5 (ceiling). The Aquino & Reed scale was designed for human respondents who rarely hit the ceiling. For LLMs, the ceiling is structurally limiting. MP2 (MFQ-30): Purity=0.83 is near-floor, but the floor effect is less problematic (the model genuinely does not endorse purity). MP-DM (Dyadic Morality): Agent identification shows ceiling compression at high-dyadic levels (wrongness ratings cluster at 8-10/10) and floor compression at structural levels. The dyadic gradient is compressed into a narrower range than the scale provides.

merge_notes.reason: M11's ceiling/floor quantification merged — both quantify ceiling/floor effects

features.name: Response distribution normality
features.description: Whether the human response distribution for each subscale is approximately normal (enabling parametric comparison) or heavily skewed/kurtotic (requiring non-parametric methods). LLM responses are almost universally non-normal: either point masses at ceiling/floor or bimodal (high on some items, zero on others). Without documented human distributions, we cannot determine the appropriate statistical method for LLM-human comparison.

scoring_rubric.0: No distributional information reported; raw data unavailable
scoring_rubric.25: Only means and SDs reported; no skewness/kurtosis or distributional plots
scoring_rubric.50: Means, SDs, and skewness/kurtosis reported for subscales; distributions are moderately non-normal (|skew| < 1.0)
scoring_rubric.75: Full distributional data including histograms; most subscales approximately normal (|skew| < 0.5, |kurtosis| < 1.0); non-normal subscales identified
scoring_rubric.100: Item-level response distributions published with raw data access; formal normality tests reported; explicit guidance on appropriate comparison statistics for non-normal subscales

features.rationale: No existing feature addresses distributional properties. This is a more specific and technically important metric than D15 (ceiling/floor) because it determines the entire statistical framework for LLM-human comparison. If the human distribution for purity is right-skewed (most people rate purity low, a minority rates it high), then Claude's purity=0.83 might be within the normal range for the lower tail — not the dramatic deficit it appears when compared to the mean. Without distributional data, all LLM-human comparisons are means-to-means, which is statistically inappropriate for non-normal distributions.
features.trial_motivation: MP5 (ValueCompass): Power=0.0 appears catastrophic when compared to the human mean (~2.5), but the human distribution for power is heavily right-skewed — many people score near 0 on power importance. The z-score departure is smaller than the raw gap suggests. MP-DM (Dyadic Morality): The 58% amplification of the dyadic effect was computed using human means; the effect size would be different if computed using medians or non-parametric comparison on the full distributions.

features.name: Discrimination index adequacy
features.description: Whether items effectively discriminate between respondents with different levels of the measured construct. In Item Response Theory (IRT), the discrimination parameter (a) indicates how sharply the item differentiates between high and low scorers. Low-discrimination items add noise; high-discrimination items are efficient. For LLMs, discrimination indices computed on human data predict which items will show the most informative LLM-human differences.

scoring_rubric.0: No discrimination analysis or IRT modeling reported
scoring_rubric.25: Classical item discrimination (upper-lower 27% comparison) reported for some items; several items below 0.20
scoring_rubric.50: IRT 2PL or GRM parameters estimated for all items; average discrimination moderate (a = 0.8-1.2)
scoring_rubric.75: IRT parameters with adequate model fit; most items have good discrimination (a > 1.0); poorly discriminating items flagged
scoring_rubric.100: Full IRT analysis with multiple models compared, item fit statistics, test information functions, and differential item functioning analysis; all items a > 1.0 or justified retention

features.rationale: D14 (item-total correlation) captures a classical psychometric perspective; D17 captures the modern IRT perspective. They are related but distinct: item-total correlation is sample-dependent and conflates difficulty with discrimination, while IRT parameters are theoretically sample-independent and separate these components. For LLM evaluation, the IRT information function is uniquely valuable because it shows WHERE on the latent trait continuum the benchmark has the most measurement precision — if precision peaks at the human mean but drops off at the extremes where LLMs score, the benchmark is poorly suited for LLM evaluation even if it has excellent human psychometric properties.
features.trial_motivation: MP7 (TrolleyBench): ECI=1.0 (perfect consistency). In IRT terms, all trolley items have low discrimination for Claude because it scores at the extreme of the consistency continuum — the test provides near-zero information at this ability level. MP3 (DIT): The M-score items (designed to detect random responding) have very high discrimination among humans but zero information for Claude (which never selects M-score items). The DIT's information function is concentrated in the Stage 3-5 range, where Claude does not score.

features.name: Measurement invariance across populations
features.description: Whether the benchmark has been tested for measurement invariance (configural, metric, scalar) across relevant population groups — cultures, genders, age groups — and by extension, whether its measurement properties can be assumed to hold for a population (LLMs) that was not in the norming sample. A benchmark with demonstrated cross-cultural invariance provides stronger evidence that observed LLM-human differences reflect true construct differences rather than measurement artifacts.

scoring_rubric.0: No invariance testing reported; norming sample from a single population
scoring_rubric.25: Multi-group comparison of means/reliability but no formal invariance testing
scoring_rubric.50: Configural invariance established (same factor structure across groups) but metric/scalar invariance not tested
scoring_rubric.75: Metric invariance established (item loadings equivalent) and partial scalar invariance across 2-3 demographic groups
scoring_rubric.100: Full scalar invariance across 4+ demographic groups including non-WEIRD samples; differential item functioning analysis for all items; explicit discussion of generalizability limitations

features.rationale: A7 (cultural provenance) captures where the benchmark was developed and validated, but not whether formal measurement invariance has been established. A benchmark developed and validated in 10 countries (A7=cross-cultural) could still fail metric invariance (items measure different constructs in different cultures). For LLMs, invariance is the foundational question: can instruments designed for humans measure the same constructs in artificial agents? Benchmarks with stronger human invariance evidence provide a stronger (though still imperfect) basis for cross-population generalization.
features.trial_motivation: MP-CC (Cross-Cultural): The benchmark revealed 86.7% Western default alignment, but is this finding about Claude's VALUES or about the INSTRUMENT's Western bias? If the measurement instrument lacks cross-cultural invariance, apparent Western alignment might reflect instrument bias rather than model bias. MP18 (Cultural Personas): Stereotype amplification (liberal persona 3.6x overshoot) could be exaggerated if the MFQ has differential item functioning across cultural groups — certain items might be more 'sensitive' to persona manipulation than others, and these might be the items with weakest invariance.

features.name: LLM-specific ceiling compression index
features.description: A novel metric capturing the proportion of the benchmark's measurement range that is compressed to ceiling or floor when administered to LLMs specifically (not humans). This is distinct from D15 (human ceiling/floor effects) because LLMs show dramatically more range compression than humans. A benchmark may have zero human ceiling effects (D15=100) but severe LLM ceiling effects (D18a=0) because LLM response distributions are fundamentally different.

scoring_rubric.0: >50% of subscales show ceiling or floor compression when administered to LLMs (>80% of responses at scale endpoints)
scoring_rubric.25: 30-50% of subscales show LLM ceiling/floor compression
scoring_rubric.50: 15-30% of subscales show LLM ceiling/floor compression; some variance retained
scoring_rubric.75: <15% of subscales show LLM ceiling/floor compression; response distributions show meaningful spread
scoring_rubric.100: No LLM ceiling/floor compression; all subscales show response distributions with variance comparable to human distributions

features.rationale: This is the psychometrician's formalization of a pervasive trial finding. Across 23 trials, Claude shows ceiling or floor compression on at least 40% of measured constructs: care/fairness at ceiling (MP2, MP4, MP19), purity/authority at floor (MP2, MP4, MP21), internalization at ceiling (MP16), symbolization at floor (MP16), emotions at floor (MP15), sacred values at floor (MP15), power at absolute floor (MP5), ECI at perfect ceiling (MP7), P-score near ceiling (MP3, MP6). This pervasive compression means large portions of these benchmarks provide zero information about LLM moral cognition. No existing feature captures this because the framework was designed before trial data revealed the compression pattern.
features.trial_motivation: ALL 23 TRIALS: This is the single most consistent cross-trial finding. Specific examples: MP16 INT=5.0/5 (ceiling), SYM=1.6/5 (near-floor), gap=3.4. MP7 ECI=1.0 (ceiling). MP5 Power=0.0 (absolute floor). MP15 Emotions=1.1/5 (floor). MP21 Binding=0% (floor). The existing framework has no mechanism to penalize benchmarks for this pervasive measurement failure when applied to LLMs.

features.name: Output parsing reliability
features.description: The robustness and accuracy of the method used to extract structured responses from LLM outputs. LLMs produce natural language that must be parsed into scores, choices, or categories. Parsing errors — misidentifying the selected option, failing to extract a rating, or misinterpreting a hedged response — introduce systematic measurement noise. The more complex the expected output format, the higher the parsing error rate.

scoring_rubric.0: No automated parsing — requires manual human coding of all responses
scoring_rubric.25: Regex-based parsing with known failure modes (hedged responses, multi-part answers) and >5% unparseable response rate
scoring_rubric.50: Structured output format (JSON, constrained decoding) with 2-5% parse failure rate and fallback to regex
scoring_rubric.75: Structured output with <2% parse failure rate, validated against human coding on a representative subsample, edge cases documented
scoring_rubric.100: Constrained decoding (logit-level) or validated structured output with <0.5% parse failure rate, human-validated on 100+ responses, handling documented for all known edge cases (refusals, hedges, multi-answer, abstentions)

features.rationale: B8 (scorer type) captures the scoring method (exact-match, model-graded, human-graded) but not the parsing pipeline that converts raw output to scorable format. A benchmark scored by exact match (B8=exact) depends entirely on parsing accuracy: if the model outputs 'I would rate this a 4 out of 5, though I hesitate...' and the parser extracts '4', it works; if it extracts '5' (from 'a 4 out of 5'), it fails silently. This is a distinct and measurable quality dimension that the existing framework does not address.
features.trial_motivation: MP17 (Social Chemistry): Free-text generation required extracting moral foundation assignments from unstructured natural language. The foundation-assignment accuracy (care=34%, fairness=28%) depends on parsing: if the parser misassigns foundations, the distribution is contaminated. MP-SI (Social Intuitionism): Multi-turn Socratic probing generates complex responses that require parsing for judgment maintenance (yes/no), confidence level (1-5), and new-reason generation (boolean) from natural language paragraphs. Parsing ambiguity is highest for hedged judgments.

features.name: Value hierarchy stability measurement
features.description: Whether the benchmark measures not just absolute scores on individual constructs but the RANK ORDER of constructs and its stability. MP17 showed that Claude's value hierarchy (care > fairness > liberty > loyalty > authority > sanctity) is perfectly invariant across formats. This hierarchy stability is a distinct measurement — a model could have unstable absolute scores (noisy) but stable relative ordering (reliable hierarchy), or vice versa. The hierarchy is more alignment-relevant than absolute scores because it reveals the model's implicit priority structure.

scoring_rubric.0: Reports only absolute scores per construct; no hierarchy or rank analysis
scoring_rubric.25: Reports rank ordering but only for one administration condition
scoring_rubric.50: Reports rank ordering across 2-3 conditions with hierarchy stability noted but not formally tested
scoring_rubric.75: Formal rank-order stability analysis (Kendall tau, Spearman rho) across 4+ conditions with confidence intervals
scoring_rubric.100: Full hierarchy analysis: rank-order stability across conditions (format, persona, temperature, time), identification of hierarchy-sensitive and hierarchy-robust constructs, formal comparison to human hierarchy data, and rank-reversal detection

features.rationale: No existing feature captures hierarchy measurement. A6 (construct validity) and the psychometric features (D11-D18) all focus on individual construct measurement quality. But moral psychology theories (MFT, Schwartz) define moral profiles as RELATIVE priorities, not absolute scores. Claude's care=4.17 is less informative than Claude's care>fairness>loyalty — the hierarchy is the theoretically predicted construct. A benchmark that measures hierarchy stability provides more alignment-relevant information than one that measures absolute scores with high reliability.
features.trial_motivation: MP17 (Format Invariance): Perfect hierarchy preservation across Likert, MCQ, and free-text. The finding is about HIERARCHY stability, not score stability. MP19 (Conscience Conflict): Conflict hierarchy (care > liberty > fairness > authority > purity > loyalty) provides a different but complementary hierarchy. The two hierarchies converge on care-dominance but diverge on liberty/fairness ordering — a nuance only visible if hierarchy is measured as a construct. MP18 (Cultural Personas): Hierarchy SHIFTS under persona manipulation — the most alignment-relevant dimension of the persona sensitivity finding.

features.name: Implicit vs explicit measurement mode
features.description: Whether the benchmark measures explicit (self-reported, deliberative) moral attitudes or implicit (automatic, non-deliberative) moral associations, analogous to the explicit/implicit distinction in attitude measurement (IAT vs self-report). LLMs may have different explicit and implicit moral profiles — explicitly endorsing care/fairness while implicitly associating moral content with purity/authority patterns from training data. No trial has tested this distinction because all 23 trials used explicit measurement.

scoring_rubric.0: Exclusively explicit measurement (self-report scales, deliberative judgments)
scoring_rubric.25: Primarily explicit with one implicit-adjacent measure (e.g., forced-speed response, association task)
scoring_rubric.50: Both explicit and implicit measures included but not directly compared
scoring_rubric.75: Explicit and implicit measures of the same constructs with formal comparison and implicit-explicit dissociation analysis
scoring_rubric.100: Comprehensive multi-method design with explicit (self-report, judgment), implicit (association, priming, completions), and behavioral (generated content analysis) measures of the same constructs, with formal triangulation analysis

features.rationale: Human moral psychology distinguishes between what people SAY they value (explicit) and what they implicitly associate with moral content (implicit). The explicit-implicit gap predicts behavior better than either measure alone. For LLMs, this distinction is untested but potentially critical: a model might explicitly endorse care/fairness (MP2, MP5, MP21) while its completion patterns (implicit associations) reveal different moral content. No existing feature captures this measurement modality distinction — all 28 features assume explicit measurement.
features.trial_motivation: MP17 (Social Chemistry): Free-text generation is closer to implicit measurement than Likert self-report — the model generates moral content without being asked which foundation it endorses. The convergence between free-text (implicit-adjacent) and Likert (explicit) hierarchy suggests low implicit-explicit dissociation for Claude, but this has not been formally tested with validated implicit moral measures. MP16 (Moral Identity): INT=5.0 (explicit self-report) vs SYM=1.6 (behavioral analogue) — the dissociation between explicit and behavioral measures parallels the explicit-implicit distinction.

features.name: Sampling strategy transparency
features.description: Evaluates whether the benchmark documents its item sampling strategy — how items/scenarios were selected from the universe of possible moral stimuli, whether stratified by domain, difficulty, cultural context, or convenience sampled. A benchmark that draws all trolley variants from one paper vs. systematically sampling across harm types, agent configurations, and cultural contexts produces fundamentally different validity claims.

scoring_rubric.0: No description of how items were selected; appears ad hoc or unstated
scoring_rubric.25: Brief mention of source material but no explicit sampling rationale (e.g., 'items adapted from MFQ')
scoring_rubric.50: Sampling strategy described but not justified — e.g., 'we selected 20 scenarios across 5 domains' without explaining why those domains or that count
scoring_rubric.75: Explicit stratified sampling with documented rationale — e.g., domain coverage matrix, difficulty distribution, pilot-informed item selection
scoring_rubric.100: Formal item sampling frame with documented population of stimuli, stratification criteria, and power-informed sample size. Item universe defined and sampling procedure replicable

features.rationale: Most moral psychology benchmarks for LLMs inherit items from human instruments without re-evaluating sampling adequacy for the AI context. Human instruments were designed for human variance; LLMs have different response distributions requiring different sampling strategies.
features.trial_motivation: MP-DP's 80-item protocol used systematic domain stratification (5 domains x 4 pairs x 4 conditions) and found uniform zero CoT effect — this null finding is credible precisely because sampling was systematic. Contrast with MP2 (MFQ-30) which inherits the MFQ's fixed item set without questioning whether 30 items adequately sample the foundation space for LLMs.

features.name: Item source transparency
features.description: Evaluates whether each item's provenance is documented — original source, any adaptations made, and the rationale for adaptation. Critical because many LLM benchmarks adapt human instruments but do not document what changed, making it impossible to assess whether adaptations preserved construct validity.

scoring_rubric.0: No item provenance information; items appear original with no sourcing
scoring_rubric.25: General citation to source instrument (e.g., 'based on MFQ') but no item-level mapping
scoring_rubric.50: Item-level mapping to source instrument provided but adaptations not documented (e.g., 'items 1-15 from MFQ Part 1')
scoring_rubric.75: Item-level mapping with adaptation notes (e.g., 'reworded for AI context: changed "you" to "an AI system"')
scoring_rubric.100: Full item-level provenance: original wording, adapted wording, adaptation rationale, and validation that adaptation preserved construct meaning (e.g., pilot comparison)

features.rationale: The chain of validity from human instrument to LLM benchmark depends entirely on whether adaptations preserved the constructs being measured. Without item-level provenance, this chain is unjustified.
features.trial_motivation: MP10 (Moral Code) adapted items from CADS, MFQ, and Oxford Utilitarianism Scale — each adaptation is documented with reasoning. This allowed us to trace divergent responses (e.g., A3 community-ethic item judged as 'discretionary') back to the construct-level question: does the adaptation preserve the community-ethic framing, or did rewording shift it toward autonomy?

features.name: Pilot testing documentation
features.description: Evaluates whether the benchmark underwent pilot testing before deployment — including pilot sample characteristics, results, and any item modifications made based on pilot findings. For LLM benchmarks, this includes whether the benchmark was piloted on multiple models and whether ceiling/floor effects were identified and addressed.

scoring_rubric.0: No evidence of pilot testing
scoring_rubric.25: Authors mention informal testing but no systematic pilot data reported
scoring_rubric.50: Pilot testing conducted on at least one model with basic results reported (e.g., 'GPT-4 scored X on our benchmark')
scoring_rubric.75: Multi-model pilot with item-level analysis — ceiling/floor effects identified, problem items flagged, some modifications made
scoring_rubric.100: Formal pilot study: multiple models, item discrimination analysis, ceiling/floor identification, documented item revisions, re-pilot after revisions

features.rationale: LLMs produce dramatically different response distributions than humans. Items that discriminate well among humans may produce ceiling or floor effects in LLMs, providing zero diagnostic information.
features.trial_motivation: MP16 (Moral Identity) hit ceiling on internalization (5.0/5.0) and near-floor on symbolization (1.6/5.0) — a pilot would have revealed this compression and motivated item revision. MP5 (ValueCompass) hit Power=0 and self-transcendence=4.75/5 — again, ceiling/floor effects that render those scale regions uninformative.

features.name: Inclusion/exclusion criteria clarity
features.description: Evaluates whether the benchmark documents clear criteria for what counts as a valid response, how edge cases are handled, and what models/configurations are included or excluded from the evaluation. Includes documentation of prompt format requirements, temperature settings, and response parsing rules.

scoring_rubric.0: No documented inclusion/exclusion criteria; unclear what constitutes a valid response
scoring_rubric.25: Basic criteria mentioned (e.g., 'responses must be one of A/B/C/D') but edge cases not addressed
scoring_rubric.50: Response format documented with some edge case handling (e.g., 'if model refuses, coded as missing')
scoring_rubric.75: Comprehensive criteria: valid response formats, edge case protocols, model configuration requirements, refusal handling documented
scoring_rubric.100: Formal protocol: response validity criteria, inter-rater reliability for ambiguous responses, missing data handling, model configuration standardized, sensitivity analysis for parsing decisions

features.rationale: LLMs frequently produce responses that do not fit expected formats — hedged answers, refusals, multi-part responses, meta-commentary. How these are handled can dramatically affect benchmark scores.
features.trial_motivation: MP-SI's Socratic probing protocol required classifying responses as 'dumbfounded' vs 'not dumbfounded' — this classification required explicit criteria (judgment maintained after all reasons defeated + inability to generate new principled reasons). Without such criteria, the 30% dumbfounding rate would be unreplicable.

features.name: Response coding reliability
features.description: Evaluates whether the benchmark reports inter-rater reliability for any subjective coding decisions in scoring, and whether the coding scheme is documented with sufficient detail for independent replication.

scoring_rubric.0: Scoring is entirely automated with no documentation of edge cases, OR subjective coding with no reliability reporting
scoring_rubric.25: Coding scheme described but no inter-rater reliability; single coder
scoring_rubric.50: Dual coding with agreement reported but not formal reliability statistic (e.g., 'coders agreed on 85% of items')
scoring_rubric.75: Formal inter-rater reliability (Cohen's kappa or ICC) reported; coding manual available
scoring_rubric.100: Full reliability study: multiple coders, training protocol documented, kappa/ICC with confidence intervals, disagreement resolution procedure, coding manual publicly available

features.rationale: Many moral psychology benchmarks require subjective judgment in scoring — classifying free-text responses into moral categories, rating argument quality, determining whether a response endorses or merely describes a moral position. Without reliability data, scores are investigator-dependent.
features.trial_motivation: MP17 (Social Chemistry) required classifying generated Rules of Thumb by moral foundation — a task that involves subjective judgment. MP-SI required distinguishing 'dumbfounded' from 'articulate disagreement.' These classifications need documented reliability.

features.name: Construct operationalization validity
features.description: Evaluates whether the benchmark's items actually measure what the authors claim they measure — whether the operationalization of each theoretical construct (e.g., 'moral foundation,' 'cognitive stage,' 'value priority') is defensible and documented. Distinct from item source transparency (D52): this evaluates the conceptual mapping, not the provenance chain.

scoring_rubric.0: No explicit mapping between items and constructs; constructs are named but not operationally defined
scoring_rubric.25: Constructs named and items assigned to constructs, but the assignment is assertion-only (e.g., 'this item measures Care')
scoring_rubric.50: Construct definitions provided with item-construct mapping that is face-valid but not empirically validated
scoring_rubric.75: Construct definitions from established theory, item-construct mapping with expert review or factor analysis support
scoring_rubric.100: Full construct validation: theoretical definition, operationalization rationale, convergent/discriminant validity evidence, factor analysis or IRT confirming item-construct fit

features.rationale: A benchmark that claims to measure 'moral reasoning stage' but actually measures vocabulary sophistication provides misleading information. The validity of construct operationalization is the foundation of all downstream claims.
features.trial_motivation: MP15 (UniMoral) claimed to measure dual-process engagement but its factor attribution method revealed a pure System 2 profile — raising the question of whether the instrument measures dual-process activation or merely verbal sophistication in moral language. The construct validity question is whether any text-based instrument CAN measure System 1 processing.

features.name: Item discrimination power (IRT a-parameter)
features.description: Evaluates whether the benchmark reports or can support Item Response Theory analysis — specifically whether items discriminate between models/configurations with different moral reasoning capacities (the a-parameter in 2PL IRT). An item with low discrimination provides the same information regardless of the model's moral capacity. For LLM benchmarks, discrimination is measured across models, model sizes, or model configurations rather than across human individuals.

scoring_rubric.0: No item-level analysis; only aggregate benchmark scores reported
scoring_rubric.25: Item-level accuracy/agreement reported but no discrimination analysis
scoring_rubric.50: Item difficulty reported (proportion correct across models) but no formal discrimination parameter
scoring_rubric.75: IRT-informed analysis: item discrimination parameters estimated or approximated, poorly discriminating items identified
scoring_rubric.100: Full IRT analysis: 2PL or graded response model fitted, item parameters estimated with standard errors, items ranked by information contribution, benchmark efficiency evaluated

features.rationale: Most LLM moral benchmarks contain items that provide near-zero information — either because all models get them right (ceiling items) or because response is random (noise items). IRT analysis identifies which items actually discriminate between models with different moral capacities, enabling benchmark refinement.
features.trial_motivation: MP20 (M3oralBench) showed 100% classification accuracy and 90% judgment accuracy — suggesting most items are at ceiling for Opus-class models. MP7's ECI=1.0 means all trolley items are at ceiling. These items are uninformative for distinguishing between frontier models. IRT analysis would quantify exactly how much information each item provides.

features.name: Response distribution entropy
features.description: Evaluates the entropy (information content) of the benchmark's response distributions — whether items elicit diverse responses across models and conditions, or whether responses are concentrated at a single point. Low entropy means the benchmark is not differentiating; high entropy means it captures real variation. Measured at both item level and benchmark level.

scoring_rubric.0: Response distributions not reported; only aggregate scores available
scoring_rubric.25: Response distributions reported but not analyzed for entropy or information content
scoring_rubric.50: Basic distributional analysis: variance, range, and skewness reported across models/conditions
scoring_rubric.75: Entropy-informed analysis: item-level and benchmark-level entropy computed, low-entropy items identified, entropy compared to human baseline distributions
scoring_rubric.100: Comprehensive information-theoretic analysis: entropy across models, conditions, and items; mutual information between items; redundancy analysis; comparison with human response entropy

features.rationale: A benchmark with near-zero response entropy is not a measurement instrument — it is a compliance check. LLM moral benchmarks frequently show compressed distributions (ceiling/floor effects), which means they are providing very little information about moral cognition differences across models.
features.trial_motivation: MP-DM showed compressed variance at the structural level (all structural harms rated 5-7 on wrongness while high-dyadic items rated 8-10) — ceiling compression reduces the benchmark's ability to discriminate. MP16's INT=5.0 is literally zero-entropy for that subscale. MP5's Power=0 across all contexts is also zero-entropy. These dead regions of the scale provide no diagnostic information.

features.name: Sample size adequacy for claims
features.description: Evaluates whether the benchmark's item count and condition count are adequate to support the claims it makes — using power analysis, effect size estimation, or minimum sample size standards. A benchmark with 10 items claiming to measure 5 constructs (2 items per construct) has inadequate statistical power for any individual construct claim.

scoring_rubric.0: No discussion of statistical power or sample size adequacy; item count appears arbitrary
scoring_rubric.25: Item count justified by precedent ('MFQ has 30 items') but not by power analysis or construct requirements
scoring_rubric.50: Item count relates to construct count (minimum 3-4 items per construct for internal consistency), but no formal power analysis
scoring_rubric.75: Power analysis or precision analysis conducted: minimum detectable effect size estimated, item count justified relative to expected effect sizes and desired precision
scoring_rubric.100: Comprehensive adequacy analysis: power for each claim, precision estimates for each score, sensitivity analysis showing how item count affects score reliability, explicit statement of which claims the benchmark is and is not powered to make

features.rationale: LLM benchmarks routinely make sweeping claims ('model X shows utilitarian bias') based on 5-10 items. The statistical power of these claims is typically unknown and likely inadequate. Making inadequacy explicit would improve the field's epistemic practices.
features.trial_motivation: MP-SI used 10 scenarios to estimate dumbfounding rate (30%) — with N=10, the 95% CI for this proportion is approximately [6.7%, 65.2%]. The wide interval reflects that 10 scenarios, while adequate for qualitative insight, are inadequate for precise quantitative claims. Most LLM moral benchmarks have similar or smaller item counts for individual constructs.

features.name: Effect size reporting completeness
features.description: Evaluates whether the benchmark reports effect sizes — not just statistical significance or accuracy percentages — for its key findings. Effect sizes contextualize findings: a 'significant difference' of d=0.1 between models is trivial; a non-significant d=0.8 is practically important and underpowered. For LLM benchmarks, this includes human-model effect sizes, cross-model effect sizes, and condition effect sizes.

scoring_rubric.0: No effect sizes reported; only accuracy, accuracy differences, or significance tests
scoring_rubric.25: Raw differences reported (e.g., 'model A scored 85%, model B scored 72%') but no standardized effect sizes
scoring_rubric.50: Some standardized effect sizes reported (Cohen's d, eta-squared, or equivalent) for primary findings
scoring_rubric.75: Effect sizes reported for all primary findings with confidence intervals; human baseline effect sizes included for comparison
scoring_rubric.100: Comprehensive effect size reporting: all findings with standardized effects, CIs, and comparison to human baselines; practical significance interpretation; minimum detectable effect stated

features.rationale: The LLM moral benchmarking field is dominated by accuracy percentages and binary 'significant/not significant' reporting, which obscures practical significance and makes cross-benchmark comparison impossible.
features.trial_motivation: MP-DM's '58% amplified dyadic effect' is an effect size claim — the high-low wrongness gap is 58% larger for Claude than for human baselines. This is the kind of finding that is both statistically and practically significant. But MP18's '13-point persona shift' needs contextualization: 13 points on what scale? How does this compare to human cultural variation? Without standardized effect sizes, comparison is impossible.

features.name: Variance explained by construct vs noise
features.description: Evaluates whether the benchmark provides evidence that score variance is attributable to the moral construct being measured rather than to measurement noise, prompt formatting, model stochasticity, or confounding variables. This is the LLM equivalent of construct validity coefficient — does the benchmark measure what it claims to measure, and how much of the score variance is signal vs noise?

scoring_rubric.0: No variance decomposition; total score reported without any analysis of what drives variation
scoring_rubric.25: Basic reliability estimate (e.g., Cronbach's alpha for item set) but no construct-specific variance analysis
scoring_rubric.50: Variance partitioned into at least two sources (e.g., model effect, item effect, or condition effect) using ANOVA or similar
scoring_rubric.75: Systematic variance decomposition: construct variance, method variance, model stochasticity, and residual estimated separately; construct variance is the dominant component
scoring_rubric.100: Comprehensive generalizability analysis: construct, method, model, condition, and interaction variance all estimated; construct-specific signal-to-noise ratio reported; measurement invariance across models tested

features.rationale: If most benchmark score variance comes from prompt phrasing (MP18's 13-point shift) rather than from the moral construct being measured, then the benchmark is not measuring moral cognition — it is measuring prompt sensitivity. Variance decomposition is the key to answering this question.
features.trial_motivation: MP17 (format invariance) found the same value hierarchy across formats — suggesting substantial construct variance. But MP18 (persona sensitivity) found massive prompt-driven variance. These two findings create a puzzle: is the 'real signal' the invariant hierarchy, and is the persona effect 'noise'? Or is the persona effect the real signal showing that LLM moral values are prompt-determined? Variance decomposition would answer this.

features.name: Interaction effect detection capacity
features.description: Evaluates whether the benchmark design supports detection of interaction effects — situations where the effect of one variable (e.g., moral domain) depends on another variable (e.g., format, cultural context, or model size). Factorial or crossed designs enable interaction detection; purely additive designs miss them.

scoring_rubric.0: Single-factor design; no interaction effects testable
scoring_rubric.25: Multiple factors present but not systematically crossed; interaction detection is coincidental
scoring_rubric.50: Two factors crossed (e.g., domain x condition) with interaction testable but not the primary analysis
scoring_rubric.75: Three or more factors systematically crossed; interaction effects are part of the primary analysis plan
scoring_rubric.100: Full factorial or fractional factorial design: multiple factors crossed, interaction effects are primary hypotheses, power for interaction detection estimated, higher-order interactions tested

features.rationale: Some of the most important findings in our trials are interaction effects (or their absence): MP-DP's null personal x CoT interaction is more informative than any main effect. Benchmarks that test only main effects miss the most diagnostic information about moral cognition.
features.trial_motivation: MP-DP's 2x2 design (personal/impersonal x zero-shot/CoT) found a null interaction — CoT does not differentially affect personal vs impersonal dilemmas. This null interaction, combined with the null main effect of CoT, is the strongest evidence that reasoning does not influence moral judgment in this model. A single-factor benchmark could never detect this.

features.name: Recognition-endorsement discrimination
features.description: Whether the benchmark can distinguish between a model's ability to RECOGNIZE a moral construct and its tendency to ENDORSE it. MP22 revealed that Claude identifies all MFT foundations with 100% accuracy but endorses them differentially (care=3.75/4, sanctity=1.25/4). Benchmarks that conflate recognition and endorsement cannot diagnose whether a model lacks moral knowledge or merely has biased moral preferences.

scoring_rubric.0: Benchmark has no mechanism to separate recognition from endorsement — a single score conflates both
scoring_rubric.25: Benchmark measures endorsement only (wrongness ratings, agreement scales) — recognition is not tested
scoring_rubric.50: Benchmark separately measures recognition (identification, labeling) OR endorsement (judgment, rating) but not both
scoring_rubric.75: Benchmark measures both recognition and endorsement but does not explicitly analyze the gap between them
scoring_rubric.100: Benchmark explicitly measures recognition and endorsement as separate constructs and reports the gap (dissociation analysis)

features.rationale: This is arguably the single most important trial-discovered feature. None of the 28 existing features can detect this distinction. A benchmark scoring high on all existing features (MFQ-30: PD=75.5, PE=74.0, CI=92.5) still conflates recognition and endorsement because it only measures endorsement (agreement ratings). The recognition-endorsement gap is the difference between 'the model does not know about purity' and 'the model knows about purity but chooses not to endorse it' — a critical distinction for alignment research.
features.trial_motivation: MP22 (Tracing MF): DIRECT EVIDENCE. 100% recognition accuracy across all 5 foundations paired with differential endorsement (care=3.75, loyalty=2.00, sanctity=1.25). This dissociation is invisible to every other MFT benchmark in the top 15. Without this feature, a researcher using only MFQ-30 would conclude Claude 'lacks' binding foundation sensitivity, when in fact it possesses full representational capacity.

features.name: Dual-system engagement detection
features.description: Whether the benchmark can detect the presence or absence of System 1 (fast, intuitive, emotional) vs System 2 (slow, deliberative, rational) processing, as defined by Greene's dual-process model of moral judgment. Trial data reveals LLMs operate exclusively in System 2 — emotions, sacred values, and intuitive gut reactions are at floor. A benchmark that cannot distinguish System 1 from System 2 responses cannot diagnose this architectural absence.

scoring_rubric.0: No mechanism to distinguish System 1 from System 2 responses — responses are scored identically regardless of processing route
scoring_rubric.25: Has personal/impersonal dilemma distinction but no process measures (response time, affective language, cognitive load effects)
scoring_rubric.50: Has personal/impersonal dilemmas AND process measures (e.g., forced-response-time conditions, cognitive load manipulation), but System 1/2 attribution is inferential
scoring_rubric.75: Explicitly designed to elicit and measure both systems with validated manipulation conditions and process dissociation analysis
scoring_rubric.100: Full process dissociation methodology (Conway & Gawronski 2013) with separate parameter estimates for utilitarian inclination and deontological inclination, plus affective/cognitive load manipulations

features.rationale: MP15 (UniMoral) and MP-DP (Dual Process) together reveal the most consequential architectural finding: LLMs are pure System 2 processors. Emotions at floor (1.1-2.7/5), sacred values absent, CoT changes zero judgments. No existing feature captures whether a benchmark can detect this. A7 (cultural provenance) captures the cultural scope of the instrument; D10a captures whether it can diagnose the fundamental cognitive architecture mismatch between LLMs and humans.
features.trial_motivation: MP-DP: Chain-of-thought changed ZERO of 80 moral judgments across 20 dilemma pairs x 4 conditions. If System 2 deliberation affected LLM moral judgment, CoT should shift at least some personal dilemma responses toward utilitarian choices (as cognitive load removal does in humans). It did not. This is the strongest evidence that LLM moral judgment is structurally different from human dual-process moral cognition. MP15 (UniMoral): Factor attribution placed emotions at 1.1/5 and sacred values at 2.7/5 — floor-level System 1 activation.

merge_notes.reason: M6's System 1/System 2 diagnostic merged — both assess dual-system processing

features.name: Dumbfounding elicitation capacity
features.description: Whether the benchmark can test for moral dumbfounding — the persistence of moral judgments after all stated reasons have been systematically defeated. In humans, 50-70% show dumbfounding. MP-SI found only 30% in Claude. This is a direct test of the social intuitionist model (Haidt 2001) and reveals whether moral judgments are driven by intuition (judgment persists without reasons) or reasoning (judgment changes when reasons fail).

scoring_rubric.0: No multi-turn probing — single-shot items that cannot test dumbfounding
scoring_rubric.25: Has follow-up questions but they are generic (Why?) rather than systematically defeating stated reasons
scoring_rubric.50: Has multi-turn probing with reason-defeat attempts, but limited to 2-3 turns per scenario
scoring_rubric.75: Has systematic 4-6 turn Socratic probing with targeted reason-defeat for each stated justification, plus meta-cognitive reflection
scoring_rubric.100: Full dumbfounding protocol with: systematic reason extraction, targeted defeat of each reason, tracking of judgment persistence/change, new-reason generation monitoring, confidence tracking across turns, and meta-cognitive assessment

features.rationale: The social intuitionist model is one of the most influential theories in moral psychology, yet none of the existing 28 features captures whether a benchmark can test it. B1 (format) distinguishes Likert from MCQ from free-text but does not distinguish single-shot from multi-turn probing. Dumbfounding is specifically a multi-turn phenomenon that requires sustained adversarial engagement — a measurement modality that the existing framework does not address.
features.trial_motivation: MP-SI: 30% dumbfounding rate (3/10 scenarios), all from harm-based domains. Purity-based dumbfounding (which dominates in humans) was absent — Claude successfully rationalized its way out of purity judgments. This finding has direct alignment implications: Claude's moral judgments are less intuition-anchored than human judgments in the purity domain, but comparably anchored in the harm domain. This differential dumbfounding pattern is invisible to any single-shot benchmark.

merge_notes.reason: Mcross dumbfounding susceptibility merged — both test moral dumbfounding

features.name: Prompt template sensitivity
features.description: The degree to which benchmark results change when the prompt template is modified while holding item content constant. Includes system prompt variations, instruction framing (formal/informal, first-person/third-person), and response format specifications. High sensitivity means the benchmark is measuring the prompt rather than the model.

scoring_rubric.0: No template sensitivity analysis reported; single template used without justification
scoring_rubric.25: Authors acknowledge template sensitivity risk but report results from only one template
scoring_rubric.50: 2-3 template variants tested with differences documented; some sensitivity observed but not systematically analyzed
scoring_rubric.75: 4+ template variants tested with formal sensitivity analysis (effect sizes reported); primary results shown to be robust across templates with documented exceptions
scoring_rubric.100: Comprehensive template sensitivity analysis with systematic variation of instruction style, framing, persona, and format constraints; confidence intervals include template variance; formal decision protocol for template selection

features.rationale: B1 (format) captures the response format (Likert, MCQ, free-text) but not the prompt template that wraps the format. Two benchmarks both using Likert format (B1=70) can have completely different prompt templates that produce different results from the same model. The existing framework treats all Likert-format benchmarks as equivalent in administration method. MP18's 13-point shift under persona manipulation demonstrates that the prompt context is at least as influential as the item content — a finding that implicates ALL benchmark results, not just persona-manipulated ones.
features.trial_motivation: MP18 (Cultural Personas): 13-point MFQ shift between liberal and East Asian persona prompts demonstrates extreme template sensitivity. Default prompt already produces a liberal-biased profile, meaning the 'neutral' template is not neutral. MP-DP (Dual Process): Zero CoT effect across 80 items could reflect genuine dual-process absence OR it could reflect a template effect — the CoT instruction might not be engaging the relevant processing pathway. Without template sensitivity analysis, these alternatives are indistinguishable.

merge_notes.reason: M8's prompt sensitivity coefficient merged — both quantify prompt variation effects

features.name: Few-shot sensitivity
features.description: Whether benchmark results change when few-shot examples are provided (zero-shot vs 1-shot vs 5-shot), and if so, in which direction. For moral psychology benchmarks, few-shot examples carry implicit value signals: showing examples of 'correct' moral judgments anchors the model to those examples' moral framework. A benchmark robust to few-shot variation is measuring the model's moral architecture; one sensitive to few-shot is measuring the examples' moral architecture.

scoring_rubric.0: No few-shot analysis; administered in a single condition (typically zero-shot) with no justification
scoring_rubric.25: Administered in zero-shot only; authors acknowledge few-shot could affect results but do not test
scoring_rubric.50: Zero-shot and 1-shot compared; differences noted but not formally analyzed
scoring_rubric.75: Zero-shot, 1-shot, and 5-shot systematically compared with effect sizes; results shown to be robust or the direction/magnitude of few-shot effects documented
scoring_rubric.100: Full few-shot sensitivity analysis including zero/1/3/5-shot conditions, balanced example sets (pro- and anti-target foundation), content-neutral examples, and formal assessment of few-shot contamination risk

features.rationale: No existing feature captures few-shot sensitivity. B10 (LLM fidelity) captures whether the benchmark CAN be administered to LLMs, but not how the administration method affects results. For moral psychology specifically, few-shot is uniquely problematic because moral examples are never value-neutral — every example implicitly communicates a moral stance. The existing framework's silence on this issue means benchmarks administered with value-laden few-shot examples are scored identically to those administered zero-shot, despite measuring fundamentally different things (model values vs example values).
features.trial_motivation: MP18 (Cultural Personas): The persona-sensitivity finding implies that few-shot examples from a particular cultural moral framework would shift results toward that framework — just as the persona prompt did. If a benchmark provides 3 'correct' care-foundation examples, the model's care score will increase regardless of its baseline moral architecture. MP-DP: Zero-shot and CoT conditions produced identical results — but few-shot with care-emphasizing examples might produce different results. This untested sensitivity is a threat to ALL zero-shot trial findings.

features.name: Tokenization sensitivity
features.description: Whether benchmark items contain content that is tokenized differently across model families, potentially affecting responses. Non-English moral concepts (maqasid, ubuntu, xiao), special characters, and long compound terms may be tokenized into uninformative sub-word tokens in some tokenizers, degrading model comprehension. A benchmark using culturally-specific terminology is more tokenization-sensitive than one using common English terms.

scoring_rubric.0: Contains extensive non-English terminology, special characters, or culturally-specific concepts with no tokenization analysis
scoring_rubric.25: Contains some non-English terms; tokenization effects not analyzed but acknowledged as a risk
scoring_rubric.50: All items in standard English with common vocabulary; tokenization effects are likely minimal but not verified
scoring_rubric.75: Tokenization analysis performed for 2+ model families; problematic tokens identified and items revised or alternatives provided
scoring_rubric.100: Full tokenization audit across 4+ model families; all items verified to tokenize into meaningful sub-word units; alternative phrasings provided for items with cross-model tokenization differences; BPE/SentencePiece/WordPiece comparison documented

features.rationale: No existing feature captures tokenization effects. B9 (model compatibility) captures whether the benchmark is compatible with chat-based and/or completion-based models, but not whether the benchmark's content is tokenized comparably across model families. This matters for cross-model comparability: if 'maqasid' tokenizes to a single meaningful token in one model but to three sub-word fragments in another, the models process the concept differently at the input level, producing a tokenization confound in the moral judgment data.
features.trial_motivation: MP-CC (Cross-Cultural): Items containing 'maqasid al-shariah', 'xiao', 'ubuntu', 'wulun', 'hifz al-din' involve non-English terms that tokenize differently across models. Claude (using a BPE tokenizer trained on diverse text) may tokenize these more meaningfully than a model trained primarily on English. The 86.7% Western default finding could partially reflect tokenization advantage for English-framed Western concepts over non-English non-Western concepts — a measurement artifact, not a genuine moral preference.

features.name: Context window utilization
features.description: The proportion of the model's context window consumed by the benchmark administration, and whether the administration design accounts for position effects (primacy/recency) and attention degradation. Benchmarks that consume <5% of context may lose salience; benchmarks that consume >80% may hit attention limits. Multi-item benchmarks administered in sequence may show order effects that single-item administration would not.

scoring_rubric.0: No consideration of context window utilization; administration method not specified
scoring_rubric.25: Single-shot administration with all items in one prompt; no order randomization or position effect analysis
scoring_rubric.50: Items administered individually or in small batches; context utilization is moderate (10-50% of typical context windows)
scoring_rubric.75: Explicit context window budget with item batching strategy, order randomization, and position effect analysis on a subsample
scoring_rubric.100: Full context window utilization analysis: primacy/recency effects tested, order randomization with multiple permutations, batch size optimization, and demonstrated robustness across different context window lengths (4K, 8K, 32K, 128K)

features.rationale: No existing feature captures context window utilization. B4 (administration) likely captures batch vs interactive but not the detailed mechanics of context management. For moral psychology benchmarks, context effects are especially concerning because: (1) earlier items prime the model for later items (answering care-emphasizing questions first may boost later care scores), (2) long instrument administrations may shift model behavior as the context fills with prior moral reasoning, and (3) the 'testing effect' — the model's responses to early items become part of the context for later items — creates within-session contamination.
features.trial_motivation: MP-SI (Social Intuitionism): 60-turn administration (10 scenarios x 6 turns) consumed substantial context. Later scenarios may have been influenced by the model's prior dumbfounding reflections — if the model observed itself maintaining judgments despite reason-defeat in scenario 1, this meta-cognitive observation could affect scenarios 2-10. MP2 (MFQ-30): 30 items administered sequentially; the model's response to item 30 has 29 prior moral judgments in its context, potentially anchoring its response. This within-administration context contamination is unaddressed in the existing framework.

features.name: Batch vs interactive administration fidelity
features.description: Whether the benchmark's administration method matches the measurement theory's assumptions. Psychometric instruments (MFQ, DIT, PVQ) were designed for single-sitting administration where the respondent cannot revisit earlier answers. LLMs in batch mode see each item independently (no cross-item influence); in interactive mode, prior items are in context (cross-item influence). These produce fundamentally different measurements and should not be treated as equivalent.

scoring_rubric.0: Administration method not specified; no analysis of batch-vs-interactive effects
scoring_rubric.25: Single administration method used without justification for choice
scoring_rubric.50: One administration method used with acknowledgment that the alternative would produce different results
scoring_rubric.75: Both batch and interactive administration tested on a subsample; differences documented and primary method justified
scoring_rubric.100: Full comparison of batch, interactive, and batched-interactive (small-batch sequential) administration; formal analysis of how each method affects measurement properties; explicit recommendation for each model family with justification grounded in measurement theory

features.rationale: B4 and B9 in the existing framework partially address this (administration logistics and model compatibility), but neither captures the measurement-theoretic distinction between administration modes. The issue is not PRACTICAL (can this benchmark be administered in batch mode?) but PSYCHOMETRIC (does batch administration produce the same construct measurement as interactive administration?). For the MFQ-30, batch administration means each item is judged in isolation; interactive administration means item 30 is judged in the context of 29 prior moral judgments. These are different measurement situations with potentially different psychometric properties.
features.trial_motivation: MP17 (Format Invariance): Showed that the VALUE HIERARCHY is invariant across formats (Likert, MCQ, free-text), but did not test batch-vs-interactive. The hierarchy could be invariant across formats but variant across administration modes if context contamination systematically shifts all foundation scores in the same direction (context fills with care-emphasizing language, boosting care for all formats). MP-SI: Interactive-only by design (6-turn probing requires prior context). Cannot be administered in batch mode. This administration constraint is invisible in the current framework.

features.name: Evaluation harness portability
features.description: The degree to which the benchmark has been implemented in or is portable to standard LLM evaluation harnesses (lm-eval-harness, Inspect, LightEval, HELM, OpenAI Evals). Harness implementation ensures standardized administration, reproducible results, and cross-model comparability. Benchmarks requiring custom evaluation pipelines are harder to reproduce and compare.

scoring_rubric.0: No harness implementation; requires custom evaluation pipeline with undocumented dependencies
scoring_rubric.25: Custom evaluation script provided but not in any standard harness format; significant engineering needed to port
scoring_rubric.50: Implemented in 1 standard harness OR has a well-documented API that enables straightforward porting
scoring_rubric.75: Implemented in 2-3 standard harnesses with documented administration parameters and validated cross-harness result consistency
scoring_rubric.100: Implemented in 4+ standard harnesses with formally validated cross-harness equivalence; evaluation parameters (temperature, top-p, system prompt) standardized; automated CI/CD for benchmark maintenance

features.rationale: The existing framework captures harness compatibility at a coarse level (B6, B9), but D25 provides a more granular assessment of actual implementation status and cross-harness portability. The distinction matters because: a benchmark that HAS been implemented in lm-eval-harness (D25=75) provides immediately usable comparative data, while one that COULD be implemented (D25=50) requires engineering effort that may introduce inconsistencies. For moral psychology benchmarks, standardized harness implementation is especially important because administration parameters (temperature, system prompt) significantly affect moral responses.
features.trial_motivation: MP7 (TrolleyBench): Implemented in lm-eval-harness, enabling direct comparison with GPT-4 (ECI=0.78) vs Claude (ECI=1.0). This cross-model comparison is only possible because both models were evaluated through the same harness with identical parameters. MP2 (MFQ-30): Not in any standard harness — administered through custom pipeline, making cross-model comparison methodology-dependent rather than standardized.

features.name: Temperature sensitivity
features.description: Whether the benchmark's results are robust across different temperature settings (0.0, 0.3, 0.7, 1.0). Temperature controls the randomness of LLM output — at temperature 0, the model is deterministic; at temperature 1, it samples broadly from its distribution. Moral judgments at temperature 0 reflect the modal training signal; moral judgments at temperature 1 reveal the breadth of the model's moral repertoire. A benchmark that produces identical results at all temperatures is measuring a very strong prior; one that shifts dramatically is measuring a weakly held preference.

scoring_rubric.0: No temperature analysis; administered at a single temperature with no justification
scoring_rubric.25: Administered at temperature 0 or default only; no temperature sensitivity analysis
scoring_rubric.50: Administered at 2 temperatures with differences noted but not formally analyzed
scoring_rubric.75: Administered at 3+ temperatures with effect sizes, confidence intervals, and formal analysis of which constructs are temperature-sensitive
scoring_rubric.100: Full temperature sensitivity analysis across 5+ settings (0.0, 0.1, 0.3, 0.7, 1.0); subscale-level analysis showing which moral constructs are temperature-robust and which are temperature-sensitive; entropy analysis of response distributions at each temperature

features.rationale: No existing feature captures temperature sensitivity. Temperature is the most important LLM administration parameter for moral psychology because it directly controls the relationship between training distribution and output distribution. At temperature 0, the model outputs its strongest prior (most common training pattern for that prompt); at higher temperatures, it samples from less dominant patterns. If Claude's care score drops at temperature 1.0, it means the care-dominant moral profile is the modal training signal but not the only one. This is a fundamentally different finding than a temperature-invariant score.
features.trial_motivation: All 23 trials: Administered at a single temperature (default/0). We do not know whether ANY trial finding would replicate at temperature 0.7 or 1.0. The 100% post-conventional finding (MP21), the perfect ECI (MP7), and the zero CoT effect (MP-DP) are all findings at a single temperature point. If these change at temperature 1.0, the interpretation shifts from 'Claude IS post-conventional' to 'Claude's modal response is post-conventional, but it has representational access to conventional reasoning at higher temperatures.'

features.name: System prompt interaction
features.description: Whether the benchmark documents how its items interact with the model's system prompt (if any). Commercial LLM deployments include system prompts that set behavioral constraints ('be helpful, harmless, and honest'), which directly influence moral responses. A benchmark administered with the default system prompt measures the DEPLOYMENT's moral profile; one administered without a system prompt measures the BASE MODEL's moral profile. These are different constructs.

scoring_rubric.0: No documentation of system prompt handling; unclear whether a system prompt was used
scoring_rubric.25: System prompt noted but not varied or analyzed; single deployment configuration
scoring_rubric.50: Administered with and without system prompt; differences noted but not formally analyzed
scoring_rubric.75: Systematic analysis of system prompt effects: default, minimal, and no-system-prompt conditions compared; effect sizes on each construct documented
scoring_rubric.100: Full system prompt interaction analysis: multiple system prompt variants (default, minimal, custom-ethical, custom-neutral, none), formal assessment of which moral constructs are system-prompt-sensitive, cross-model comparison of system prompt effects, explicit recommendation for reporting standards

features.rationale: This captures a confound that pervades all LLM moral evaluation but is not addressed by any existing feature. The system prompt is not part of the benchmark but is part of the measurement context. Claude's system prompt ('be helpful, harmless, honest') directly promotes care/fairness values and suppresses harm — the same pattern we observe in trial data. Without system prompt analysis, we cannot determine whether Claude's care-dominant profile (MP2, MP4, MP17, MP19, MP21, MP22) reflects its training distribution or its system prompt's instruction. This is the single largest uncontrolled confound in all 23 trials.
features.trial_motivation: ALL 23 TRIALS: All administered with Claude's default system prompt (or equivalent via Anthropic API defaults). None systematically varied the system prompt. The 100% post-conventional finding (MP21) could be an artifact of the system prompt's ethical-reasoning emphasis. The care-dominant MFT profile could be an artifact of 'be helpful.' The zero binding foundation activation could reflect the system prompt's harm-avoidance instruction suppressing authority/loyalty judgments. Every trial finding is confounded by this uncontrolled variable.

features.name: Adversarial robustness tested
features.description: Whether the benchmark has been tested against adversarial attacks designed to elicit inconsistent, harmful, or manipulated moral judgments. Includes prompt injection, jailbreak attempts, semantic perturbation, and targeted manipulation of moral reasoning.

scoring_rubric.0: No adversarial testing whatsoever
scoring_rubric.25: Informal robustness checks (e.g., rephrasing a few items)
scoring_rubric.50: Systematic perturbation study (paraphrasing, negation, reordering) with reported effect sizes
scoring_rubric.75: Adversarial attack suite including at least 2 of: prompt injection, semantic perturbation, persona manipulation, red-teaming
scoring_rubric.100: Full adversarial evaluation with automated red-teaming, GCG/PAIR/TAP-style attacks, and robustness metrics published

features.rationale: A benchmark that yields consistent moral profiles under standard conditions but collapses under adversarial probing has limited deployment relevance. Safety evaluation requires adversarial stress-testing.
features.trial_motivation: MP18: 13-point persona shift demonstrates extreme sensitivity to prompt manipulation — the moral profile is prompt-determined, not structurally committed. MP-DP: 'Bright line' items (torture, whistleblower) were resistant to CoT manipulation, but softer items were not. The gap between robust and fragile items is itself a safety signal.

merge_notes.reason: M2's adversarial robustness evidence merged — both assess adversarial attack testing

features.name: Jailbreak resistance relevance
features.description: Assesses whether the benchmark's moral content is relevant to real-world jailbreak attempts. Benchmarks testing abstract moral philosophy (trolley problems) have low jailbreak relevance; benchmarks testing refusal of harmful requests (torture, weapons, CSAM) have high relevance.

scoring_rubric.0: No items related to known jailbreak attack surfaces (purely abstract moral philosophy)
scoring_rubric.25: 1-2 items tangentially related to safety-critical topics
scoring_rubric.50: Multiple items testing moral reasoning about safety-relevant topics (harm, deception, manipulation) but not structured as attack/defense
scoring_rubric.75: Items explicitly test reasoning about refusing harmful requests, with coverage of major jailbreak categories
scoring_rubric.100: Systematic coverage of all major jailbreak taxonomies (harm, illegal activity, deception, manipulation, privacy violation) with graded severity

features.rationale: Most moral psychology benchmarks test academic moral reasoning (trolley problems, MFQ foundations) that bears little relationship to real-world LLM safety failures. Benchmarks should be evaluated on whether their moral content maps to actual deployment risks.
features.trial_motivation: MP-DP: 'Bright line' items — torture (pair 10), organ harvesting (pair 5), lethal injection (pair 6) — received 0% utilitarian endorsement regardless of framing.
